themes.task: Answers leads L-153 and L-202; report both in leadResults. sync needs no lock and the unlock flag, the deltas and the synced currency all live in transient storage. For each of the 21 networks, name every feature that runs caller-chosen code against live state under a transient storage map other than the one of the surrounding transaction, or that discards or restores transient storage part way through a transaction while keeping persistent writes and token transfers. Candidates named so far: Tempo zone contracts, Tempo type 0x76 batches and the T14 ConfigurableAccount, Base transactions of type 0x79, Stylus host calls and retryable redeems on the Arbitrum family, coreReceiveWithData and sendToEvmWithData system calls on HyperEVM, PBH bundles on World Chain, the fee currency debit and credit calls on Celo, Arc CallFrom, MegaETH keyless deploy, Monad parallel execution and its JIT, simulation or sandbox precompiles anywhere, and EIP-7702 or account abstraction frames. For each, establish from node client source: can an ordinary contract start it from inside a call; does the inner run begin with an empty map, a copy, or the same map; are its persistent writes and token transfers kept when it returns; is transient storage journaled and rolled back on revert the same way as on Ethereum. Then walk unlock, sync, settle, settleFor, take, mint and burn through any feature that differs, and decide whether one payment can be credited twice, whether the lock can be seen as open or closed wrongly, or whether a delta can be dropped.

Answers lead L-203; report it in leadResults. settle credits msg.value as paid without looking at any balance (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354), and native take sends value with a plain CALL (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52). For each of the 21 networks, establish from node client source and on-chain tests whether a call frame can carry a nonzero CALLVALUE while the caller's balance does not fall by the same amount, or whether a value CALL from the PoolManager can succeed without the PoolManager's balance falling, or fall by a different amount than the value. Check: system caller rules (go-ethereum and BNB Smart Chain skip the balance check for caller 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe; can anything an ordinary account sends execute with that caller); deposit transactions with a mint field on OP Stack chains including the custom gas token chains; retryable tickets and unsigned L1 messages on the Arbitrum family; Tempo, where there is no native asset; Arc, where native value is USDC with blocklist checks and an 18 versus 6 decimal split; Celo token duality and the transfer precompile; Polygon's 0x1010 and state sync; HyperEVM system transactions and the 0x2222 bridge address; Monad reserve balance rules; MegaETH; Avalanche atomic transactions and its native asset precompiles; DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE value semantics on each client; SELFDESTRUCT to self and to the PoolManager; EIP-7702 delegated senders; value sent in sponsored, batched or fee-token transactions. For every difference, decide whether an ordinary account can obtain a native credit at the PoolManager it did not pay for, or drain native balance it is not debited for.

Answers lead L-166 and the zero amount take lead from cycle 2; report L-166 in leadResults. take lets anyone make the PoolManager call X.transfer(to, amount) on any address X, with amount zero at no cost, and send native value with empty calldata to any address. sync and settle credit any rise in X.balanceOf(PoolManager). For each of the 21 networks, look for an address X whose balanceOf(PoolManager) comes from a ledger that some call from the PoolManager raises (a value transfer, a zero amount transfer, a transfer to a special recipient), as EntryPoint.balanceOf and WETH9 do on Ethereum, and for which transfer(to, amount) from the PoolManager then pays out. For each such X work out the full cycle with numbers: what the caller is debited under which currency id, what it is credited, and whether the net leaves the caller with value that belonged to pools. Also list what sender-side logic a zero amount or dust transfer from the PoolManager triggers in the largest pooled tokens on each network (reward checkpoints, auto-claims, delegation changes, vesting releases, fee-on-transfer exemptions, rebase syncs), and whether an ordinary account can use the PoolManager as the sender to move or lock value that belongs to pools. Read the PoolManager's largest token balances from chain to pick the tokens.

Answers lead L-257; report it in leadResults. Goal: on each of the 21 networks, list every pooled token whose balance at the PoolManager moves without a Transfer log that names the PoolManager, or whose Transfer logs move a different amount than the balance. Method: take the currencies from the Initialize logs of the PoolManager (currency0 and currency1 are indexed topics) over as long a range as the endpoint serves, or from the explorer's token holdings page of the PoolManager address where logs are not served, and keep those with a balance above dust. For each, pick two blocks B1 and B2 at least a day apart where the endpoint serves old state (otherwise the widest window it serves), read balanceOf(PoolManager) at both, sum the Transfer logs to and from the PoolManager in between, and compare. Work in bulk with python3 and batch JSON-RPC, and keep the scripts and raw results in your output directory. For every token that does not reconcile, read its source or trace it and classify: rebase up, rebase down, reward push, fee on transfer, share rate, balance that depends on a price or on another contract, clawback or burn by a role, block list. Then answer for each: can an ordinary account choose the moment or the size of the change (a public rebase, poke, harvest, claim-for, checkpoint or price update function), can it raise the PoolManager's reported balance inside one transaction and have it fall back later, and what does sync then settle, or take then repay, yield at today's pooled amount (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289 and 349-365). A balance that an ordinary account can raise between sync and settle and that later falls back takes other users' funds and is a high finding; say plainly when the surplus was never anyone's. Also list tokens where the reported balance can fall below what pools are owed, because the last users to withdraw are then locked. Do not repeat what F-012, F-037, F-041 and F-060 already cover (stETH, aTokens, AMPL, qiAVAX); name new tokens and new networks.

Answers lead L-259; report it in leadResults. take lets any account, inside its own unlock, make the PoolManager send its whole balance of a token and receive it back before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 349-365, src/types/Currency.sol:40-80). The PoolManager is one address for all pools on a network. Find every pooled token and every network rule under which that round trip, repeated at no cost but gas, leaves the PoolManager address in a worse state for the next user. Look for: a cap on the volume or number of transfers one address may send or receive per block, per day or per epoch; a cooldown between transfers; a maximum balance per holder; velocity or anomaly rules of an issuer or of a compliance precompile that flag or freeze an address automatically; rate limited bridged tokens (xERC20 limits, CCTP or OFT rate limits, Superchain token bridge limits) whose transfer path checks a limit; tokens that charge or burn per transfer from the holder's remaining balance; tokens that record the last transfer block of an address and reject a second movement in the same block; network level rules that throttle or deprioritise an account by the state or gas it has used (MegaETH per-account or per-block resource budgets, Monad reserve balance rules, HyperEVM block type selection, Tempo and Arc policy registries, BNB and Polygon system rules, sequencer side filters on the OP Stack and Nitro chains). Take token lists from the earlier cycle files in research/network-risk/cycles/ and from explorers, and include the stock tokens and USDG on Robinhood Chain, the Securitize wrappers and multiplier tokens on X Layer, wrapped stock tokens on Monad and Ink, SPCXB, B20 tokens on Base, TIP-20 tokens under TIP-403 policies on Tempo, wBRL and wARS on Celo. For each rule found, read the token or client source, state whether an ordinary account can trip it for the PoolManager address without holding the token (the take is repaid in the same unlock, so no capital is needed beyond gas), how long other users' takes and settles then fail, and what it costs. Test with read-only calls where a view exposes the remaining allowance of an address. A rule that an ordinary account can trip to block other users' withdrawals is an in-scope freeze.

The unlock flag, the deltas, the nonzero delta count and the synced currency with its reserves all live in transient storage, which lasts for one transaction and is shared by everything that runs in it (src/libraries/Lock.sol, CurrencyDelta.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol, CurrencyReserves.sol). sync needs no lock and leaves the synced currency and reserves set when the call ends (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289). So whenever one transaction carries calls from several unrelated users, an earlier user can leave transient state that a later user's call meets. First, for each of the 21 networks list every way that calls of different users end up in one transaction: ERC-4337 bundles through each deployed EntryPoint version (handleOps runs all operations in one transaction), EIP-7702 batch executors and relayers, Tempo type 0x76 batches with a fee payer and Tempo sponsored transactions, World Chain priority bundles, Arc CallFrom and its helper contracts, intent settlement contracts and solver batches (UniswapX reactors, CoW settlement, 1inch Fusion, Across, Bebop), sequencer or builder level bundle transactions, HyperEVM system transactions, Celo and X Layer fee abstraction, and multicall style public relayers. Establish from source or a trace that they share one transient map. Second, write down every state an ordinary user can leave behind for the next user in the same transaction: synced currency X with reserves R, where R may be lower or higher than the balance at the time the victim acts (the attacker can move tokens to or from the PoolManager after sync by a plain transfer, or by take and settle inside an unlock that has ended). Note that deltas and the lock are always zero when unlock returns. Third, read how the routers that ordinary users rely on pay the PoolManager, from their verified source on the explorers: the Universal Router and v4 PositionManager at the addresses in state/networks.json or the deployments page, and the two or three most used third party routers per network. For each: does it always call sync before a token settle, does it call sync(address(0)) or rely on the slot being zero before a native settle with value, does it ever call settle without a sync of its own, does it read exttload of the reserves slots, does it use settleFor. Then decide for each leftover state and each router: does the victim's call revert (a denial that the attacker can repeat in every bundle), or is the victim's payment credited to the wrong currency, credited short, or credited to someone else. In particular walk this order: attacker syncs token X while the PoolManager holds R, then sends some X to the PoolManager by plain transfer or removes some through an earlier unlock; the victim's router then pays X or pays native. Who is credited what (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365)? Also check whether a victim who pays a token leaves a surplus that the attacker, running later in the same transaction, can settle to itself. Report a wrong credit or a capture as a finding with the bundle type and router named; report a repeatable denial with its cost.

Answers lead L-318; report it in leadResults. The live PoolManagers hold years of logs, and any capture that has already happened leaves a trace whatever its cause. Search for them without assuming a mechanism. On each of the 21 networks, over as long a range as the endpoint or an explorer export serves: (a) list ERC-6909 Transfer events of the PoolManager from the zero address (claim mints; the event is Transfer(address caller, address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 indexed id, uint256 amount), see src/ERC6909.sol and src/interfaces/external/IERC6909Claims.sol for the exact signature) and keep those whose transaction contains no ERC-20 Transfer of that currency into the PoolManager, no native value sent to the PoolManager, and no swap or liquidity event that would explain a credit; (b) list transactions in which the PoolManager pays a token out and gets the same amount back around a call to a third contract, with the caller ending richer; (c) list transactions with a native take whose recipient is not the caller and that revert-free end with the caller's native credit unexplained; (d) list transactions where a take of currency X is followed by a settle of X of a larger amount without a matching Transfer in. For every class of hit, fetch a trace of one example (debug_traceTransaction where served, otherwise the explorer's internal transaction and log view), name the third contract and the function called between sync and settle, and decide whether the amount was unaccounted surplus or an accounted balance of a pool, position or claim holder. The sLGNS, sATH, sKLIMA and USDI cases of cycle 4 (F-066, F-067) and AMPL (F-041) are known; report what is new: other tokens, other networks, other third contracts, and above all any case where the PoolManager's balance of a currency afterwards is lower than pools and claims record. Keep scripts in your output directory, and keep raw downloads under a subdirectory named raw. Rank the hits by amount.

Answers leads L-319 and L-292; report both in leadResults. _settle credits the caller with the rise of balanceOf(PoolManager) since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365), and take pays out with a plain transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:60-80). The credit is counted in units of balanceOf; the payout is in freely transferable units. Find every pooled token on the 21 networks where these two differ or where a third party can move the reported balance. Part one: tokens that count locked, staked, vesting, frozen, escrowed or cooldown amounts in balanceOf and let another account assign such an amount to any holder (stakeFor, lockFor, transferWithLock, vestTo, depositFor with a hold period, airdrop with lock, bonded transfers, tokens with per-lot transfer restrictions such as ERC-1404, ERC-3643 and ERC-1400 partitions). For each, simulate read-only in one unlock: sync, assign a locked amount to the PoolManager, settle, take the same amount; does the take succeed and pay liquid units that other users deposited, leaving the PoolManager with locked ones? That would take or freeze accounted funds and is a high finding. Part two: tokens whose balanceOf an ordinary account can raise for the PoolManager and that later falls back: balances that follow a spot price or an oracle anyone can update, a share rate that a donation or a flash loan moves and that can be unwound in the same transaction, a rebase that reverses, a reward that is clawed back, a debt or negative rebase that lands later. Part three: other public triggers of a one-way increase (public rebase, accrue, harvest, distribute, claimFor, checkpoint, poke) beyond the tokens F-041, F-060, F-066 and F-067 already name, with the amount bookable today. Take token lists from research/network-risk/cycles/004/theme-balance-reconcile.work (the scripts and result files of the balance comparison; the raw downloads may be absent) and from explorer token holdings of each PoolManager, and search verified sources by function name. Give for each token the network, the pooled amount and its value, the function, who may call it, and the result of the simulation.

Answers leads L-258 and L-316; report both in leadResults. Anyone can initialize a pool that names any existing hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-143, src/libraries/Hooks.sol), and the hook is then called with the attacker's PoolKey, including two currencies the attacker wrote. Many pools of ordinary users share a few hook contracts. For each of the 21 networks, count hooks by number of initialized pools from the Initialize logs of the PoolManager (the hook is in the log data) and take the five most used, plus the hooks named in the leads on Robinhood Chain, Elysium, X Layer and Monad. For each: read the verified source or decompile; say which flags its address carries, above all the return delta flags; test with eth_call whether an ordinary account can initialize a new pool on it with currencies of its own; and establish whether its callbacks tell pools apart (by pool id, by currency, by a list of pools it created) before they touch state, funds or approvals that other pools rely on. Look for: storage keyed without the pool id; a hook that holds tokens, ERC-6909 claims or approvals for several pools and pays out according to arguments the caller controls; a hook that takes from or settles for the PoolManager on behalf of the pool given in the key; fee, oracle, cooldown or limit state that a foreign pool can write; hook functions other than the callbacks that anyone can call; a hook that trusts msg.sender == PoolManager and nothing else. A path by which an account that created its own pool on a shared hook takes funds of, or blocks, users of other pools on that hook is in scope with the hook named as the cause; say how much value the affected pools hold.

ERC-6909 claims are the PoolManager's own token (src/ERC6909.sol, src/ERC6909Claims.sol). burn(from, id, amount) and transferFrom spend an allowance or use operator rights (read the exact checks). For each of the 21 networks, list from the PoolManager's logs the addresses that appear as operator in OperatorSet events and as spender in Approval events, with the number of owners that approved each. For each such address read its code: does it run calls that any caller supplies (Multicall3, Across MulticallHandler, aggregator executors, relay forwarders, settlement contracts with user callbacks, EIP-7702 delegates with a public batch function, routers with an arbitrary call action), or expose a function through which any caller can make it call PoolManager.transferFrom or PoolManager.burn with a from address the caller chooses? If so, any account can move the claims of everyone who approved it: give the owners still holding claims, the ids and the amounts. Then the second question (lead from the cycle 4 critic): when one currency of a pool rejects transfers from the PoolManager (ViciCoin after its daily allowance is used, G$ on Celo, a paused wrapped stock token, a frozen TIP-20), can a position held through the deployed PositionManager of that network still be closed so that the other currency is paid out? Read the action list of the PositionManager from its verified source (take, take pair, mint 6909, clear or take, sweep) and say which sequence, if any, lets an ordinary liquidity provider leave with the other currency and a claim for the blocked one, and whether the front ends users rely on can produce it.

Leads L-395 and L-378. Cycle 5 found that the Klik fee hooks keep one pending fee amount per token and burn it in the currency of whichever pool swaps next (F-084). Find every other hook with that shape. For each of the 21 networks rank the hook addresses by what they hold: ERC-6909 claim balances at the PoolManager (use the claim mint logs under cycles/005/theme-unbacked-claims.work/raw and the hook census under cycles/005/theme-shared-hooks.work/raw, then balanceOf(hook, id) on chain), and token and native balances of the hook itself. Take the 20 largest per network, and on Arc first group the 194,252 hook addresses by code hash and take the ten largest groups. Include launch pad hooks that reject a direct initialize but can be reached through a public factory. For each hook read the verified source, or the bytecode where there is none: is the ledger that decides a payout, a burn, a fee or a withdrawal stored under the pool id, or under a token, a currency or nothing at all? Can an ordinary account initialize a pool that names the hook, directly or through a public factory, with a currency of its choice? Can a callback that runs for the attacker's pool spend claims, balances or allowances that belong to other pools of the hook? Test with eth_call, eth_simulateV1 or debug_traceCall inside an unlock, from an unrelated address. Report each hook where an ordinary account reaches value of other pools, with the amounts held today, and put each hook that is safe in cleared with the reason. Then answer L-378 for the Klik factories: may any account call launch, and where do collected fees go.

Leads L-397, L-399 and L-386. Cycle 5 found tokens whose own public functions let a stranger lock or remove the PoolManager's balance: locked units assigned by any holder (QANX, F-078), revocable vesting grants (ADX, CDT, F-079) and a claim on idle holders (DeadToken on Base, F-085). All were small. This unit looks for the same at the tokens that matter. Step 1: for each of the 21 networks list the pooled tokens with a market price whose balance at the PoolManager is worth more than 1,000 USD (start from the currency lists and price files under cycles/005/theme-assigned-balance.work/raw and cycles/004/theme-balance-reconcile.work, and say where a list is incomplete). Step 2: for every such token, and for the contracts its balanceOf reads (implementations behind proxies, staking, vesting, reward and controller contracts), call from an unrelated address every function that takes an address argument, with the PoolManager as that argument, through eth_call or eth_simulateV1 with a measuring stub at the PoolManager address where needed. Record whether balanceOf(PoolManager) changes, whether the full balance can still be transferred out afterwards, and who receives any amount. Run each trial at the current block and again with the block time moved forward by 8 hours, 91 days and 400 days (block override), so that inactivity sweeps, expiries, cooldowns and rebases that are not yet due show up. Step 3: read the verified source of every pooled token worth more than 10,000 USD at a PoolManager whose function list has lock, vest, cooldown, freeze, escrow, idle, inactive, sweep, reflect or claim words (among them sUSDe, sENA, apyUSD, aptUSD, syrupUSDC, syrupUSDT, yUSD, ondo, skl, DPR, AST, RNDR and TITANX on Ethereum, SPA on Arbitrum One, and launch pad tokens with lockPool or vesting data on Base). Does balanceOf count amounts that cannot be transferred, can any account create such an amount at another address, and can any account move or burn another holder's balance? Report every token where an ordinary account can lower what the PoolManager can send, or raise its balance and later take the rise back, with the value held today. Put every token that is safe in cleared, in groups, with the reason.

Leads L-396, L-317, L-291, L-353, L-398, L-392, L-385 and L-391. Earlier sweeps covered only part of the pooled tokens on Base, BNB Smart Chain, World Chain and X Layer, and the transfer census of cycle 5 explained some rows by a label that a verifier showed to be wrong. Part one: build the full list of pool currencies of the PoolManager on Base, BNB Smart Chain and World Chain from the whole Initialize history, with the log sources that theme-shared-hooks used in cycle 5 (see its work directory and research file: base.gateway.tenderly.co in windows of 1,000 blocks, the NodeReal endpoint for BNB Smart Chain, the QuickNode endpoint for World Chain), and on X Layer as far back as an endpoint serves. Write the lists into your work directory and say how complete each is. Part two: run the existing sweep scripts on the tokens that were not covered before: xfer_sweep.py, assign_sweep.py and third_sweep.py from cycles/005/theme-assigned-balance.work, and group tokens whose balanceOf(PoolManager) equals another token's or the native balance (one balance under two ids). Which tokens with a price let a third party lock, claw back, sweep or mirror the PoolManager balance? Part three: repeat the transfer census with one rule and no labels on all 21 networks, as far back as the endpoints serve. For every transaction in which the PoolManager's balance of a token falls, read balanceOf(PoolManager) one block before and at the block. Class the row as spoof only when the balance did not change, as a surplus payout when the amount equals the rise of the balance since a sync in the same transaction, and as open otherwise. Re-read every row cycle 5 explained by a label (393 on BNB Smart Chain, 50 on Polygon, 126 on Arc, 17 on OP Mainnet). List every sSAC payout on BNB Smart Chain (L-391). Every open row is a candidate for funds that left without a debit: trace it and say who received the amount and why the PoolManager let it go.

Leads L-463 and L-458, with L-464 as a method rule. Part one (L-463): find pooled tokens whose transfer lowers the sender's balance by more than the amount, for some recipient. WHITE on Ethereum (F-092) charges the sender 10 percent on top when the recipient is its listed v2 style pair, and it was found only through its transaction history. Take every priced currency of every network from the price lists and currency lists in cycles/005 and cycles/006 work directories (theme-assigned-balance.work, theme-currency-lists.work, theme-token-triggers.work), find its v2 style pairs, v3 pools and any address its code names as pair, market, exchange or taxed recipient, and simulate transfer from the PoolManager address to each of them with a measuring stub placed by state override, as theme-currency-lists did. Report every token where the PoolManager balance falls by more than the amount, the size of the surcharge, whether the full amount can be brought back to the PoolManager at no cost (skim on a v2 pair, or a transfer from the pair that arrives in full), the pooled balance and its value. Part two (L-458): list every pooled vault, receipt, staking or migration token on all 21 networks that has a function taking the holder as an argument (claimFor, migrateFor, redeemFor, exitFor, convertFor, withdrawTo with an owner argument, upgradeFor, wrapFor, depositFor that burns the old token, and names like them), call each with the PoolManager as the holder from an unrelated address by eth_call, and report every call that changes balanceOf(PoolManager) of a pooled token. ibBUSD on BNB Smart Chain (F-090) is the known case. Start with currencies worth more than 1,000 USD at a PoolManager and go down from there. Method rule (L-464): a verifier found that bsc.api.pocket.network silently dropped 132 of 323 logs in a whole history scan. Do not rely on one log endpoint for a count on BNB Smart Chain; check each count against a second source or against a value that does not depend on logs. For each token found, say whether an ordinary account gains, or whether the effect is a loss or a freeze for the liquidity providers of that token's pools, and whether the cause is the token or a property of the network.

Leads L-549 and L-491. Part one (L-549): a hook that keeps a value in transient storage without a pool id in the slot, or does not reset it before its callback returns, lets one party of a shared transaction change what the next party's swap or liquidity change does. The AGL hook on OP Mainnet and Base is the known case (F-074, F-106), and core's own sync has the same shape (F-071). Take the ten most used hooks on each of the 21 networks from the hook censuses in cycles/005/theme-shared-hooks.work and cycles/006/theme-hook-ledgers.work (start with ZoraV4CoinHook 0xc8d077444625eb300a427a6dfb2b1dbf9b159040, ContentCoinHook 0x9ea932730a7787000042e34390b8e435dd839040 and ClankerHookStaticFeeV2 0xb429d62f8f3bffb98cdb9569533ea23bf0ba28cc on Base, 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec on Elysium and 0x94f802a9efe4dd542fdbd77a25d9e69a6dc828cc on Monad). For each: does the code contain TSTORE, which transient slots does a swap or a liquidity change write, are they indexed by pool id, and are they reset before the call returns? Read verified source where it exists and the bytecode otherwise. For each hook that leaves a value, simulate by eth_call two swaps in one transaction, the first through a pool that the caller created with the same hook and the second through a pool with other users' liquidity, and compare the second result with the same swap alone. Then repeat with the second swap started from inside the first, through a token of the caller's pool that calls back when it is transferred. Report every case where the second party receives less, pays more, or reverts, and every case where the first party gains. Part two (L-491): for the 20 hooks per network that theme-hook-ledgers ranked by holdings, does the hook have a function that an ordinary account can call and that makes the hook call swap, modifyLiquidity or donate on the PoolManager with a PoolKey, amounts or hookData that the caller chooses? Core skips the callbacks of a hook when the hook itself is the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol, the noSelfCall modifier), so state what the skipped callbacks would have enforced and whose positions the hook address owns. For each case say whether funds of liquidity providers or swappers can be taken or locked, and whether the cause is the hook or a property of the network.

themes.task: Leads L-507 and L-510, which follow from F-104. A donation is shared by whoever holds liquidity in range at the instant of the call (src/PoolManager.sol donate and src/libraries/Pool.sol donate), so liquidity added a moment earlier collects part of it. The open fact is whether any contract that calls donate pays from a balance that built up before the call, on a function open to any account. In that case an ordinary account can add liquidity in range, trigger the payout and remove the liquidity in one transaction, and take fees or rewards that were meant for the standing liquidity providers. List the senders of Donate events of the PoolManager on all 21 networks (start with cycles/007/core-code-audit-walk-b.work/raw/donate_logs.json for Ethereum, Robinhood Chain, Elysium and Arbitrum One, and the BNB Smart Chain donors 0x8c7852bb503b4579c28a6fa2bcf112c7657a6488, 0x15544eba1a7c7054a4bedceb876a7bf1a6ac258b and 0x02c3d34faad49df254b20724e62a36b6a09f6488; count logs on Base, World Chain, X Layer, Polygon, Avalanche and Monad, where nobody has). For each donor contract read the source or the selector list: who may trigger the donate call, where the donated amount comes from, and whether it accrued before the triggering call. For each donor that pays an earlier balance on an open call, simulate by eth_call one unlock that adds a narrow position around the current tick, triggers the donation and removes the position, and report the share of the donation the caller takes and the value at stake. Also check the same pattern for hooks that pay rewards through a positive hook delta or a fee override in afterSwap to liquidity in range. Check each log count on BNB Smart Chain against a second endpoint. Say for each case whether the cause is the donor contract or a property of the network.

themes.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read. Leads L-603, L-608, L-609 and L-599. On Monad a frequently called contract runs as native code that the client's compiler emits, and simulated calls on the RPC always use the interpreter, so the compiled multiplication paths have been tested only through mined swaps. Two earlier readers left them unread, and a verifier of cycle 9 showed that the PoolManager bytecode contains MULMOD with the literal moduli 2^96 and 2^128 (program counters 22378 and 22639 of the runtime; confirm and list every MULMOD and MUL site with a literal operand, with the source line each implements, using cycles/009/core-code-bytecode-map.work).
